title: Regulatory Mechanisms of Human Activities on Riverine CO2 Emissions in Hainan Island
content:
ABSTRACT

Human activities are fundamentally altering riverine carbon cycling, yet the response of CO2 emissions to disturbance gradients in tropical island rivers remains unclear. We combined hydrochemistry, δ13CDIC and Δ14CDIC, and landscape metrics quantified across multiple riparian buffer widths to diagnose controls on CO2 emissions along three major rivers on Hainan Island, China. Downstream reaches showed higher nutrients and algal biomass (TN: 1.0 ± 0.6 mg L−1 to 2.1 ± 2.4 mg L−1; Chl-a: 2.1 ± 2.5 μg L−1 to 5.0 ± 5.3 μg L−1), consistent with nutrient enrichment and enhanced primary production. Radiocarbon signatures became less depleted downstream (Δ14CDIC: −5.9‰ to 2.4‰ in the Nandu; −59.0‰ to −21.3‰ in the Wanquan), and the modern carbon contribution increased (91.2%–96.8% and 96.2%–98.0%, respectively), indicating strengthened autochthonous production. This shift coincided with a decrease in CO2 flux (F CO2) from 235.1 to 132.5 mmol m−2 day−1, supporting the interpretation that nutrient enrichment and hydrologic regulation jointly enhanced instream carbon processing and contributed to reduced CO2 emissions. Incorporating anthropogenic intensity and riparian land use at appropriate spatial scales is therefore essential for regional river carbon budgets and mitigation planning.
